blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Elements in which the last electrons enter in d-subshell are known as d-block elements.
  • Generally, transition elements are those which have their last two shells incomplete i.e. nth and (n-1)th shell in their neutral and most stable ionic form are transition elements.
• Thus series or Zn, Cd and Hg are not transition elements.

• Note: All Transition elements are d-block elements but vice versa is not true.
Location: Found in groups 3-12 (IIIB to IIB) of the periodic table.

Electronic Configuration: Their last electrons are filled in the d-orbitals.

  • General configuration: (n-1) d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻²
  • Example: Iron - (Fe) [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² (Except Palladium)
  • Exception Cr and Cu group members (having $ns¹(n-1)d^5$ and ns¹(n-1)d¹⁰ configuration respectively)
Variation in atomic radius :

In a period: Atomic size

• Decreases from Sc to Mn (As $Z_{eff}$ dominates)

• Remain same in Fe, Co, Ni (As $Z_{eff}$ $\approx$ σ)

• Increases from Cu to Zn (σ dominates)

In a group:

• In 3rd or III B group: Increases on moving down the group 3d<4d<5d.
    • In group 4(IVB) - 12(IIB) : Increases from 3d to 4d then becomes almost equal(3d<4d≈5d) due to lanthanoid contraction.

Note: A decrease in size due to the poorest shielding of f subshell electrons is known as Lanthanoid contraction.

  • Magnetic Character: Metals, which have unpaired electrons show paramagnetism.
Ex. :  Cr - $[Ar]4s^13d^{5}$ (having unpaired e- in 4s & 3d subshell)

• Spin only magnetic moment  = √n(n+2)

here n = no. of unpaired electron.

• A diamagnetic substance is one which is slightly repelled by a magnetic field.

Ex: Zn - $[Ar]4s^23d^{10}$ (No unpaired e- thus diamagnetic)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Ionisation energy: Trends of I.E. in d block elements

  • In a period : I.E. depends on variation in size.
  • In a group : For Configuration $d^4, d^5, d^6, d^{10}$ trend of I.E. will be : 3d < 4d < 5d
Rest all except IIIB group : 4d < 3d <5d

For IIIB group : 3d > 4d > 5d

Melting Point :  Having high melting point and boiling point values of transition elements.

  • In any d-block series M.P increases up to VI B group (max. unpaired $e^-$) and then decreases.
  • Highest M.P - Tungsten (W)
  • Lowest M.P - Mercury (Hg)

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Transition elements are usually characterised by variable oxidation states but Zn does not show this property because of

(A) completion of np-orbitals

(B) completion of (n–1)d orbitals

(C) completion of ns-orbitals

(D) inert pair effect
blocks.answer:
Answer: (B) completion of (n–1)d orbitals

Zinc (Zn) has a completely filled $3d^{10} $configuration, making its (n−1)d orbitals stable and unavailable for bonding. This prevents Zn from exhibiting variable oxidation states, unlike other transition metals with partially filled (n−1)d orbitals. Zn only shows a +2 state due to the loss of $4s^2$ electrons.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
The d-block element which is a liquid at room temperature?

(A) Cu

(B) Hg

(C) Ce

(D) Pm
blocks.answer:
Answer: (B) Hg (Mercury)

Mercury is the only d-block element that is a liquid at room temperature (melting point: $−38.83^∘C$ ). This is due to weak metallic bonding caused by its completely filled $5d^{10}$ configuration, which limits electron delocalization.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing Trends: Misinterpreting atomic and ionic radius trends across the series, forgetting that radii decrease slightly due to increasing nuclear charge and ineffective shielding by d-electrons.
  • Overlooking Exceptions: Ignoring irregularities in ionization energy (e.g., Cr and Cu) caused by the stability of half-filled (3d⁵) and fully filled (3d¹⁰) subshells.
  • Generalizing M.P. Trends: Assuming melting points increase uniformly, ignoring that they depend on the number of unpaired d-electrons and metallic bonding strength (e.g., Mn has an unexpectedly low melting point).
  • Misunderstanding Shielding: Misinterpreting the weak shielding effect of d-electrons, leading to errors in predicting trends in radii and ionization energy.
  • Forgetting Oxidation States: Overlooking the impact of variable oxidation states on ionization energy and physical properties.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text: Variable oxidation states possible are:

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
Which of the following oxidation states is most commonly observed in d-block elements?

(1) +1

(2) +2

(3) +3

(4) +4
blocks.answer:
Answer:
(2) +2

Solution:
The +2 oxidation state is common because most d-block elements lose their two 4s-electrons first when forming ions. This state is particularly stable for elements like Fe, Co, Ni, and Zn.
blocks.prompt: Which of the following oxidation states is most commonly observed in d-block elements?

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
Which of the following d-block elements does not exhibit the +2 oxidation state?

(1) Scandium (Sc)

(2) Iron (Fe)

(3) Copper (Cu)

(4) Zinc (Zn)
blocks.answer:
Answer:
(1) Scandium (Sc)

Solution:
Scandium predominantly exhibits the +3 oxidation state. It does not exhibit +2 because after losing its 4s and 3d electrons, it attains a stable noble gas configuration (Ar).
blocks.prompt: Which of the following d-block elements does not exhibit the +2 oxidation state?

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Assuming all d-block elements exhibit similar oxidation states.
  • Forgetting exceptions like Cr and Cu families.
  • Overlooking trends in stability of +2 and +3 states.
  • Confusing variable oxidation states with charge density trends.

Promoted iron is used in the Haber-Bosch process for making NH₃.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
The Ziegler-Natta catalyst used for the polymerisation of ethene and styrene is TiCl4 + (C2H5)3Al, the catalysing species (active species) involved in the polymerisation is

(1) TiCl4

(2) TiCl3

(3) TiCl2

(4) TiCl
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is:

(2) TiCl₃

Explanation:

In Ziegler-Natta catalysts, TiCl₄ reacts with the organoaluminum compound (C₂H₅)₃Al to produce the active species. During this reaction, a chlorine atom is abstracted from TiCl₄ by (C₂H₅)₃Al, reducing titanium from a +4 oxidation state to a +3 oxidation state. The resulting species, TiCl₃, is the active catalytic species that facilitates the polymerization of ethene and styrene by coordinating with the monomers and enabling their addition to the growing polymer chain.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
The catalytic activity of transition metals depends on :

(1) Their ability to exist in different oxidation states

(2) The size of the metal atoms

(3) The number of empty atomic orbitals available

(4) None of these
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is:

(1) Their ability to exist in different oxidation states

Explanation:

The catalytic activity of transition metals primarily depends on their ability to exist in multiple oxidation states, which allows them to easily facilitate redox reactions by alternating between these states. Additionally, their partially filled d-orbitals allow them to form intermediate complexes with reactants, lowering activation energy and speeding up the reaction.
options: (1) Their ability to exist in different oxidation states
(2) The size of the metal atoms
(3) The number of empty atomic orbitals available

modules.name: Density and Property Chart of D-block Elements

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• The atomic volume of the transition elements is low compared with s-block, so their density is comparatively high $(D = \frac{M}{V})$.
  • Os $(22.57 \, \text{gm cm}^{-3})$ and Ir $(22.61 \, \text{gm cm}^{-3}) $ have the highest density.
  • In all the groups (except IIIB), there is a normal increase in density from the 3d to 4d series, and from 4d to 5d, it increases just double. Due to lanthanide contraction
Example:  $Ti < Zr \ll Hf$
In the 3d series

  • Highest density: Cu and Ni
  • Lowest density: Sc
• Some important orders of density
    • Fe < Ni = Cu
    • Fe < Cu < Au
    • Fe < Hg < Au

Table

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
Why do elements of the 5d series have higher densities than the 3d and 4d series?

(1) Greater nuclear charge and smaller atomic radii

(2) Higher ionization energies

(3) Presence of more valence electrons

(4) Poor metallic bonding
blocks.answer:
Answer: (1) Greater nuclear charge and smaller atomic radii

Solution:
The 5d-series elements have higher densities because their atoms have a higher atomic mass and smaller atomic radii due to the lanthanide contraction, which leads to stronger packing in the metallic structure.
options: (1) Greater nuclear charge and smaller atomic radii
blocks.prompt: Why do elements of the 5d series have higher densities than the 3d and 4d series?

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
Which of the following d-block elements has the highest density?

(1) Iron (Fe)

(2) Tungsten (W)

(3) Osmium (Os)

(4) Gold (Au)
blocks.answer:
Answer: (3) Osmium (Os)

Solution:
Osmium has the highest density (∼22.6 g/cm³) among the d-block elements. Its small atomic volume and strong metallic bonding contribute to this property.
blocks.prompt: Which of the following d-block elements has the highest density?

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing density trends: Students often misinterpret the increasing density trend across periods, forgetting it is due to atomic mass increasing faster than atomic volume.
  • Mislinking density to electronic configuration rather than atomic packing.
  • Overlooking the role of metallic bonding strength in varying properties.
  • Ignoring anomalies like Mn and Zn due to fully filled or half-filled d-orbitals.

blocks.text:
Complex Formation: Chromate – Dichromate

Preparation:

$4FeCr_2O_4 + 8Na_2CO_3 + 7O_2 \xrightarrow{1000^\circ\text{C}-1300^\circ\text{C}, \text{red hot, air}} 8Na_2CrO_4 + 2Fe_2O_3 + 8CO_2$

8Na₂CrO₄ + 2Fe₂O₃ dissolve in water and filtered:

  • Residue (Fe₂O₃)
  • Filtrate (Na₂CrO₄).
Then,

$2Na_2CrO_4 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + Na_2Cr_2O_7 + H_2O$

Its solubility up to 32°C increases and then decreases.
Hence, a suitable temperature is to be employed to crystallize out Na₂SO₄ first.

Then, Na₂Cr₂O₇ is crystallized out as Na₂Cr₂O₇·2H₂O on evaporation (red crystal).

$\begin{aligned} &\text { How to get } \mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{Cr}_2 \mathrm{O}_7 \text { : }\\ &\underset{\text { Hot Conc. }}{\mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{Cr}_2 \mathrm{O}_7}+2 \mathrm{KCl} \xrightarrow[\text { decomposition }]{\text { double }} \mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{Cr}_2 \mathrm{O}_7+2 \mathrm{NaCl} \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Definition & General properties:

  • Elements in which the last e- enters the f subshell are known as f block elements.
  • Also known as Inner Transition metals as their ultimate, penultimate and pre-penultimate shells are incomplete.
  • Lanthanide Series : Ce(58) to Lu(71).
  • Actinide Series : Th(90) to Lr(103)
  • General electronic configuration : $(n-2)f^{1–14}, (n-1)d^{0–1},ns^2$
Lanthanide series or Lanthanides (Rare Earth Elements or Lanthanones)

  • Lanthanides are reactive elements, so they are not found in a free state in nature.

blocks.title: Oxidation States
blocks.text:
All the lanthanides attain a +3 oxidation state, and only Cerium, Praseodymium, and Terbium exhibit a higher oxidation state (+4).

(Oxidation states in brackets are unstable states)

  • All the lanthanides attain a +3 oxidation state, and only Cerium, Praseodymium, and Terbium exhibit a higher oxidation state (+4). Eu and Yb exhibit a +2 oxidation state.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Which is the most common oxidation state of lanthanides.

(1) +3

(2) +4

(3) +5

(4) +6
blocks.answer:
Ans. (1)

The +3 oxidation state arise when they lose two 6S electrons and one 5d or 4f electron, which is energetically most favorable.
blocks.prompt: Which is the most common oxidation state of lanthanides.

blocks.question:
Which among the following exhibit oxidation state higher than common oxidation state f-block

(1) Cerium

(2) Praseodymium

(3) Terbium

(4) All of the above
blocks.answer:
Answer: (4)

Solution: All of the above as all above elements shows +4 O.S. which is greater than common O.S. i.e. +3.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Manganate & Permanganate :

Properties : The above green solution is quite stable in alkali, but in pure water and in the presence of acids, it deposits and gives

$3K_2MnO_4 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2KMnO_4 + MnO_2 + 4KOH$

  • $K_2MnO_4$​ (Potassium permanganate) is purple.
  • $MnO_2​ $​ (Manganese dioxide) is dark brown.

blocks.title: Reaction
blocks.text:
Oxidising Properties of $KMnO_4$: (in acidic medium)

  • $MnO_4^- + Fe^{2+} + H^+ \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + Mn^{2+} + H_2O$
  • $MnO_4^- + I^- + H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + I_2 + H_2O$
  • $MnO_4^- + SO_2 \xrightarrow{H^+} Mn^{2+} + H_2SO_4$
  • $MnO_4^- + NO_2^- + H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + NO_3^- + H_2O$
  • $MnO_4^- + H_2C_2O_4 + H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + CO_2 + H_2O$
  • $MnO_4^- + H_2S \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + S \downarrow + H_2O$
  • $MnO_4^- + S_2O_3^{2-} \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + S_4O_6^{2-}$
  • $KMnO_4 + HCl \rightarrow KCl + Cl_2 + H_2O + MnCl_2$
Note: Permanganate titrations in presence of hydrochloric acid are unsatisfactory since hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine.

Oxidising Properties of $KMnO_4$ in neutral or faintly alkaline solution:

• $2KMnO_4 + H_2O + KI \rightarrow 2MnO_2 + 2KOH + KIO_3$
Thiosulphate is oxidised almost quantitatively to sulphate:

$8MnO_4^- + 3S_2O_3^{2-} + H_2O \rightarrow 8MnO_2 + 6SO_4^{2-} + 2OH^-$

Oxidising Properties in neutral or weakly acidic solution:

$2KMnO_4 + 3MnSO_4 + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{Zn}^{2+} \text{ or ZnO}} 5MnO_2 + K_2SO_4 + 2H_2SO_4$

or $2MnO_4^- + 3Mn^{2+} + 2H_2O \rightarrow 5MnO_2 + 4H^+$

In laboratory conversion of $Mn^{2+}$ to $MnO_4^-$ is done by:

  • Heating Effect:
$2KMnO_4 \xrightarrow{\Delta \, 200^\circ C} K_2MnO_4 \, (\text{Green}) + MnO_2 \, (\text{Black}) + O_2$

$2K_2MnO_4 \xrightarrow{\text{at red hot}} 2K_2MnO_3 + O_2$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Magnetic properties:

  • In tripositive lanthanide ions the number of unpaired electrons regularly increases from lanthanum to Gadolinium (0 to 7) and then continuously decreases up to lutecium (7 to 0).
  • lanthanum and lutecium ions are diamagnetic, while all other tripositive lanthanide ions are paramagnetic. (Exception – Neodymium is the most paramagnetic lanthanide).
  • $Ce^{4+}$ and  $Yb^{2+}$ are also diamagnetic ions.

blocks.title: Colour Properties
blocks.text:
• The lanthanide ions have unpaired electrons in their 4f orbitals. Thus, these ions absorb light in the visible region, undergo an f–f transition, and hence exhibit colour.
  • The colour exhibited depends on the number of unpaired electrons in the 4f orbitals.
  • The ions often with $ 4f^n$ configuration have a similar colour to those ions having $ 4f^{14–n}$configuration.
  • Lanthanide ions having $4f^0, 4f^{14}$ are colourless.

blocks.text:
• Confusing the magnetic behavior of lanthanides and actinides (paramagnetic vs. ferromagnetic).
  • Misunderstanding the origin of color due to f-d transitions.
  • Forgetting to account for the oxidation state’s impact on color and magnetic properties.
  • Overlooking the effect of crystal field splitting in complexes.
  • Incorrectly correlating f-block elements’ electron configurations with their properties.

blocks.text:
On moving down the group in group number 4 to 15, the decrease in size of elements of 6th period compared to elements of 5th period irrespective of increase in shell number is known as Lanthanide contraction. This is due to poorest shielding of (n-2)f electrons

Effect of Lanthanide contraction :

  • In d block elements (atomic radius): For Group 4 to 12 -->3d<4d≈5d
  • In Group 13, 14 & 15 (atomic radius)

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Actinide series Th(Z=90) to Lr(Z=103):

Oxidation states :

• In lanthanides and actinides, +3 oxidation state is the most common for both of the series of elements.

• Physical appearance: Actinides are silvery white metals. They get tarnished when exposed to the attack of alkalis.

• Density : All the actinides except thorium and americium have high densities.

• Colour: Actinide ions are generally coloured. The colour of actinide ions depends upon the number of 5f-electrons. The ions containing no unpaired 5f-electrons (exactly fully filled f-subshell) are colourless, as expected.

• Ionisation energies: Ionisation energy values of actinides are low.

• Electropositive character: All the known actinide metals are highly electropositive. They resemble the lanthanide series in this respect.

• Melting point increases with increase in atomic number.

• Magnetic properties: The actinide elements are paramagnetic due to the presence of unpaired electrons.

• Radioactive nature: All the actinides are radioactive in nature.

• Actinide contraction: The size of the atom/cation decreases regularly along the actinides series. The steady decrease in ionic radii with an increase in atomic number is referred to as actinide contraction. This is due to poor shielding of 5f electrons.

  • Magnetic Character: Metals, which have unpaired electrons show paramagnetism.
Ex. :  Cr - $[Ar]4s^13d^{5}$ (having unpaired e- in 4s & 3d subshell)

• Spin only magnetic moment  = √n(n+2)

here n = no. of unpaired electron.

• A diamagnetic substance is one which is slightly repelled by a magnetic field.

Ex: Zn - $[Ar]4s^23d^{10}$ (No unpaired e- thus diamagnetic)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Ionisation energy: Trends of I.E. in d block elements

  • In a period : I.E. depends on variation in size.
  • In a group : For Configuration $d^4, d^5, d^6, d^{10}$ trend of I.E. will be : 3d < 4d < 5d
Rest all except IIIB group : 4d < 3d <5d

For IIIB group : 3d > 4d > 5d

Melting Point :  Having high melting point and boiling point values of transition elements.

  • In any d-block series M.P increases up to VI B group (max. unpaired $e^-$) and then decreases.
  • Highest M.P - Tungsten (W)
  • Lowest M.P - Mercury (Hg)

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• The atomic volume of the transition elements is low compared with s-block, so their density is comparatively high $(D = \frac{M}{V})$.
  • Os $(22.57 \, \text{gm cm}^{-3})$ and Ir $(22.61 \, \text{gm cm}^{-3}) $ have the highest density.
  • In all the groups (except IIIB), there is a normal increase in density from the 3d to 4d series, and from 4d to 5d, it increases just double. Due to lanthanide contraction
Example:  $Ti < Zr \ll Hf$
In the 3d series

  • Highest density: Cu and Ni
  • Lowest density: Sc
• Some important orders of density
    • Fe < Ni = Cu
    • Fe < Cu < Au
    • Fe < Hg < Au

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Complex Formation: Chromate – Dichromate

Preparation:

$4FeCr_2O_4 + 8Na_2CO_3 + 7O_2 \xrightarrow{1000^\circ\text{C}-1300^\circ\text{C}, \text{red hot, air}} 8Na_2CrO_4 + 2Fe_2O_3 + 8CO_2$

8Na₂CrO₄ + 2Fe₂O₃ dissolve in water and filtered:

  • Residue (Fe₂O₃)
  • Filtrate (Na₂CrO₄).
Then,

$2Na_2CrO_4 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + Na_2Cr_2O_7 + H_2O$

Its solubility up to 32°C increases and then decreases.
Hence, a suitable temperature is to be employed to crystallize out Na₂SO₄ first.

Then, Na₂Cr₂O₇ is crystallized out as Na₂Cr₂O₇·2H₂O on evaporation (red crystal).

$\begin{aligned} &\text { How to get } \mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{Cr}_2 \mathrm{O}_7 \text { : }\\ &\underset{\text { Hot Conc. }}{\mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{Cr}_2 \mathrm{O}_7}+2 \mathrm{KCl} \xrightarrow[\text { decomposition }]{\text { double }} \mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{Cr}_2 \mathrm{O}_7+2 \mathrm{NaCl} \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Definition & General properties:

  • Elements in which the last e- enters the f subshell are known as f block elements.
  • Also known as Inner Transition metals as their ultimate, penultimate and pre-penultimate shells are incomplete.
  • Lanthanide Series : Ce(58) to Lu(71).
  • Actinide Series : Th(90) to Lr(103)
  • General electronic configuration : $(n-2)f^{1–14}, (n-1)d^{0–1},ns^2$
Lanthanide series or Lanthanides (Rare Earth Elements or Lanthanones)

  • Lanthanides are reactive elements, so they are not found in a free state in nature.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Magnetic properties:

  • In tripositive lanthanide ions the number of unpaired electrons regularly increases from lanthanum to Gadolinium (0 to 7) and then continuously decreases up to lutecium (7 to 0).
  • lanthanum and lutecium ions are diamagnetic, while all other tripositive lanthanide ions are paramagnetic. (Exception – Neodymium is the most paramagnetic lanthanide).
  • $Ce^{4+}$ and  $Yb^{2+}$ are also diamagnetic ions.

blocks.title: Colour Properties
blocks.text:
• The lanthanide ions have unpaired electrons in their 4f orbitals. Thus, these ions absorb light in the visible region, undergo an f–f transition, and hence exhibit colour.
  • The colour exhibited depends on the number of unpaired electrons in the 4f orbitals.
  • The ions often with $ 4f^n$ configuration have a similar colour to those ions having $ 4f^{14–n}$configuration.
  • Lanthanide ions having $4f^0, 4f^{14}$ are colourless.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
On moving down the group in group number 4 to 15, the decrease in size of elements of 6th period compared to elements of 5th period irrespective of increase in shell number is known as Lanthanide contraction. This is due to poorest shielding of (n-2)f electrons

Effect of Lanthanide contraction :

  • In d block elements (atomic radius): For Group 4 to 12 -->3d<4d≈5d
  • In Group 13, 14 & 15 (atomic radius)
In ≈ Tl

Sn ≈ Pb

Sb ≈ Bi

blocks.title: Key Points
blocks.text:
• Cerium is most useful element in the lanthanides –
  • Lanthanide compounds like cerium molybdate, cerium tungstate are used as paints and dyes.
  • In textile and leather industries (Ce salts).
  • Misch metal is pyrographic and is used in cigarette & gas lighter.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Actinide series Th(Z=90) to Lr(Z=103):

Oxidation states :

• In lanthanides and actinides, +3 oxidation state is the most common for both of the series of elements.

• Physical appearance: Actinides are silvery white metals. They get tarnished when exposed to the attack of alkalis.

• Density : All the actinides except thorium and americium have high densities.

• Colour: Actinide ions are generally coloured. The colour of actinide ions depends upon the number of 5f-electrons. The ions containing no unpaired 5f-electrons (exactly fully filled f-subshell) are colourless, as expected.

• Ionisation energies: Ionisation energy values of actinides are low.

• Electropositive character: All the known actinide metals are highly electropositive. They resemble the lanthanide series in this respect.

• Melting point increases with increase in atomic number.

• Magnetic properties: The actinide elements are paramagnetic due to the presence of unpaired electrons.

• Radioactive nature: All the actinides are radioactive in nature.

• Actinide contraction: The size of the atom/cation decreases regularly along the actinides series. The steady decrease in ionic radii with an increase in atomic number is referred to as actinide contraction. This is due to poor shielding of 5f electrons.

blocks.title: Uses
blocks.text:
Some important uses of actinides are as follows:

  • Thorium : Thorium is used in atomic reactors as fuel rods and in the treatment of cancer.
  • Uranium : Uranium is used as nuclear fuel. Its salts are used in glass industry (for imparting green colour), textile industry and also in medicines.
  • Plutonium : Plutonium is used as fuel for atomic reactors as well as in atomic bombs.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing Trends: Misinterpreting atomic and ionic radius trends across the series, forgetting that radii decrease slightly due to increasing nuclear charge and ineffective shielding by d-electrons.
  • Overlooking Exceptions: Ignoring irregularities in ionization energy (e.g., Cr and Cu) caused by the stability of half-filled (3d⁵) and fully filled (3d¹⁰) subshells.
  • Generalizing M.P. Trends: Assuming melting points increase uniformly, ignoring that they depend on the number of unpaired d-electrons and metallic bonding strength (e.g., Mn has an unexpectedly low melting point).
  • Misunderstanding Shielding: Misinterpreting the weak shielding effect of d-electrons, leading to errors in predicting trends in radii and ionization energy.
  • Forgetting Oxidation States: Overlooking the impact of variable oxidation states on ionization energy and physical properties.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Assuming all d-block elements exhibit similar oxidation states.
  • Forgetting exceptions like Cr and Cu families.
  • Overlooking trends in stability of +2 and +3 states.
  • Confusing variable oxidation states with charge density trends.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing density trends: Students often misinterpret the increasing density trend across periods, forgetting it is due to atomic mass increasing faster than atomic volume.
  • Mislinking density to electronic configuration rather than atomic packing.
  • Overlooking the role of metallic bonding strength in varying properties.
  • Ignoring anomalies like Mn and Zn due to fully filled or half-filled d-orbitals.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Ignoring the role of unpaired electrons and variable oxidation states in complex formation.
  • Confusing ligands and coordination numbers.
  • Misunderstanding the use of crystal field theory for explaining stability.
  • Forgetting that d-block elements form coloured complexes due to d-d transitions.
  • Overlooking the importance of hybridization in complex geometry.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing  f-block with d-block elements
  • Ignoring actinides' variable oxidation states
  • Assuming lanthanides exhibit +3 only, neglecting +2 and +4 states
  • Misidentifying f-orbitals' shielding effect
  • Overlooking similarities in chemical properties across series

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing the electronic configurations of lanthanides and actinides.
  • Overlooking the stability of higher oxidation states.
  • Misunderstanding the role of ligands in f-block complexes.
  • Ignoring the lanthanide contraction effects on complex formation.
  • Incorrectly predicting the geometries of f-block complexes.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing the magnetic behavior of lanthanides and actinides (paramagnetic vs. ferromagnetic).
  • Misunderstanding the origin of color due to f-d transitions.
  • Forgetting to account for the oxidation state’s impact on color and magnetic properties.
  • Overlooking the effect of crystal field splitting in complexes.
  • Incorrectly correlating f-block elements’ electron configurations with their properties.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing the cause of contraction – it's due to poor shielding by 4f electrons.
  • Not recognizing that the contraction occurs across the lanthanide series, affecting ionic sizes and properties.
  • Misunderstanding its impact on atomic size, ionization energy, and electronegativity trends.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Ignoring the lanthanoid contraction affects ionic size and reactivity.
  • Overlooking the role of lanthanoids in catalysis and materials science.
  • Misunderstanding the oxidation states of lanthanoids.
  • Not differentiating between the uses of lanthanoids in various industries, including electronics and medicine.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing the actinides with lanthanides, as both are f-block elements.
  • Not remembering the atomic numbers and the position of actinides in the periodic table.
  • Forgetting that actinides exhibit variable oxidation states, especially +3, +4, and +5.

blocks.text:
Manganate & Permanganate :

Properties : The above green solution is quite stable in alkali, but in pure water and in the presence of acids, it deposits and gives

$3K_2MnO_4 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2KMnO_4 + MnO_2 + 4KOH$

  • $K_2MnO_4$​ (Potassium permanganate) is purple.
  • $MnO_2​ $​ (Manganese dioxide) is dark brown.

blocks.title: Reaction
blocks.text:
Oxidising Properties of $KMnO_4$: (in acidic medium)

  • $MnO_4^- + Fe^{2+} + H^+ \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + Mn^{2+} + H_2O$
  • $MnO_4^- + I^- + H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + I_2 + H_2O$
  • $MnO_4^- + SO_2 \xrightarrow{H^+} Mn^{2+} + H_2SO_4$
  • $MnO_4^- + NO_2^- + H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + NO_3^- + H_2O$
  • $MnO_4^- + H_2C_2O_4 + H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + CO_2 + H_2O$
  • $MnO_4^- + H_2S \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + S \downarrow + H_2O$
  • $MnO_4^- + S_2O_3^{2-} \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + S_4O_6^{2-}$
  • $KMnO_4 + HCl \rightarrow KCl + Cl_2 + H_2O + MnCl_2$
Note: Permanganate titrations in presence of hydrochloric acid are unsatisfactory since hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine.

Oxidising Properties of $KMnO_4$ in neutral or faintly alkaline solution:

• $2KMnO_4 + H_2O + KI \rightarrow 2MnO_2 + 2KOH + KIO_3$
Thiosulphate is oxidised almost quantitatively to sulphate:

$8MnO_4^- + 3S_2O_3^{2-} + H_2O \rightarrow 8MnO_2 + 6SO_4^{2-} + 2OH^-$

Oxidising Properties in neutral or weakly acidic solution:

$2KMnO_4 + 3MnSO_4 + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{Zn}^{2+} \text{ or ZnO}} 5MnO_2 + K_2SO_4 + 2H_2SO_4$

or $2MnO_4^- + 3Mn^{2+} + 2H_2O \rightarrow 5MnO_2 + 4H^+$

In laboratory conversion of $Mn^{2+}$ to $MnO_4^-$ is done by:

  • Heating Effect:
$2KMnO_4 \xrightarrow{\Delta \, 200^\circ C} K_2MnO_4 \, (\text{Green}) + MnO_2 \, (\text{Black}) + O_2$

$2K_2MnO_4 \xrightarrow{\text{at red hot}} 2K_2MnO_3 + O_2$
